why: If the claim holds up, a purpose-built image classifier from a decade ago still beats general-purpose frontier LLMs on a clinical imaging task, a caution against swapping specialized diagnostic models for prompt-driven multimodal systems.
notes: Central claim: a roughly 10-year-old convolutional neural network outperforms current frontier LLMs at skin cancer diagnosis from images. No article text was available, so the dataset, model identities, metrics (sensitivity, specificity, AUC), and test protocol are unverified here.

The comparison pits a task-specific supervised CNN against general multimodal LLMs; the framing suggests specialization still wins on narrow medical imaging, but the magnitude and task definition are not confirmed from the source.
Which frontier LLMs were tested, how they were prompted, and whether they saw raw images or descriptions are not available in the provided material.
No information on sample size, class balance, or whether results are peer-reviewed versus a self-published lab write-up (hosted on lynchlab.net).
Surfaced on Hacker News at 154 points with 84 comments as of first sighting on 2026-10-25; discussion volume is a signal of interest, not of methodological rigor.
summary: A write-up hosted at lynchlab.net claims that a convolutional neural network roughly ten years old outperforms current frontier large language models at diagnosing skin cancer from medical images. The piece is used as evidence that task-specific, supervised vision models can still beat general-purpose multimodal LLMs on narrow clinical imaging tasks. The full article text was not available for this assessment, so the dataset, the specific CNN and LLMs compared, the prompting setup, and the evaluation metrics (such as sensitivity, specificity, or AUC) could not be verified. It is also unclear whether the work is peer-reviewed or a self-published lab analysis. The post drew attention on Hacker News (154 points, 84 comments) on 2026-10-25. The central claim should be treated as a self-reported result pending access to the methodology.
novelty: old specialized CNN beats frontier LLMs on medical imaging task
audience: ML practitioners skeptical of LLM-for-everything hype

title: He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art
why: The headline vendor benchmark number (90% on a math test) tells you almost nothing about a model's absolute capability, but the rank order it produces has held up across datasets for 60 years, and that load-bearing property breaks in the LLM era because builders train on different, benchmark-tuned data mixes.
notes: Moritz Hardt (Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems) argues in his 2026 book 'The Emerging Science of Machine Learning Benchmarks' that benchmarks were 'the mistake that made machine learning' and drove progress anyway, 'mostly by sheer luck.'

His central empirical claim: absolute accuracy swings wildly with small test-set changes (e.g. 90% on one dataset, 73% on a near-identical one), yet relative rankings between models stay stable across datasets, which is what let ML avoid a replication crisis. He stresses there is no comprehensive theory for why rankings stay stable.

The stability holds only under one condition: models trained on the same training set. LLMs break it because their training data is unknown and can be assembled to favor specific benchmarks, so a worse model can win by 'benchmaxxing' (post-training on earlier benchmarks); the tell is strong scores on benchmarks released before a model and weak scores on ones released just after.

Historical framing: first benchmark in 1959 (punch-card character recognition with a train-test split); 1987 DARPA speech-to-text benchmark showed AI losing to statistical methods and helped trigger an AI winter; 2012 ImageNet win by an 8-layer net started the deep learning revolution. Hardt says ML ignored the textbook 'holdout method' by publishing test sets online, enabling leakage into development loops.

Proposed fix ('altitude training', by analogy to the 1968 Mexico City 1,500m won by a high-altitude-trained Kenyan runner): drop the training set entirely, keep a test set, and add a standardized protocol that trains every model briefly on benchmark-relevant data to level the field and restore ranking validity. Caveat he concedes: this yields progress indicators, not valid absolute measurements or mechanistic understanding; he cites CASP protein folding as proof benchmarks can advance science without a prior theory.

Model names in the piece (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable) appear as the article's own examples, not products tied to cited results; all performance figures are illustrative, and no vendor methodology is examined.
summary: In a Quanta interview tied to his 2026 book 'The Emerging Science of Machine Learning Benchmarks,' Moritz Hardt argues that AI benchmarking has been broken for decades but worked anyway by luck. His key distinction: a benchmark's absolute accuracy number is unreliable (small test-set changes produce large swings and should not support claims like 'equal to an expert mathematician'), but the relative ranking of models has stayed stable across datasets for roughly 60 years, which is why ML avoided a replication crisis. That stability depends on all models sharing a training set, a condition LLMs violate because their undisclosed, benchmark-optimized data mixes let worse models win via 'benchmaxxing.' Hardt proposes replacing the training set with a standardized 'altitude training' protocol that prepares each model on benchmark-relevant data before testing, restoring ranking validity even as absolute scores inflate. He concedes this still yields only progress indicators rather than mechanistic understanding, but points to CASP protein folding as evidence that benchmarks can drive scientific gains without a prior theory. He offers no formal theory for why rankings stay stable, calling it an empirical phenomenon.
novelty: rankings are stable even when absolute benchmark scores aren't
audience: ML researchers and engineers who rely on benchmark leaderboards

title: Hackers stole millions of US military personnel records during months-long data breach
why: If you ever served or worked for the DoD, your unencrypted Social Security number, birth date, and service record sat exposed for nine months, and the Pentagon's "no evidence of misuse" comes with no stated basis.
notes: Breach ran October 2025 to mid-July 2026, exploiting a vulnerability in an unspecified file-sharing system used by the Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC); multiple unauthorized users had access.
A Pentagon official (via CNN and Federal News Network) put the scope at ~2.8M living people and close to 300,000 deceased; for context, the active-duty force was 1.3M as of March.
Exposed records were unencrypted and included SSNs, name, date of birth, sex, race, and military service details.
DMDC is the DoD's identity management provider, maintaining 60M+ records and linking personnel to smart cards, passwords, and physical/computer access to Pentagon systems, buildings, and bases.

DoD says it has no indication the data was misused but did not explain how it reached that conclusion; the attackers are unidentified, and TechCrunch got no reply on whether officials heard from them.
Follows the September 2026 FBI breach attributed to ShinyHunters and echoes the 2015 OPM breach of 22M+ records broadly attributed to China.
summary: The U.S. government is reportedly notifying millions of current and former military service members and staff that their personal data was stolen in a months-long breach of DMDC personnel records. Per a breach notice shared on Reddit, unauthorized users exploited a vulnerability in an unspecified file-sharing system between October 2025 and mid-July 2026, exposing unencrypted SSNs, names, dates of birth, sex, race, and service information. A Pentagon official cited by CNN and Federal News Network said the breach affects about 2.8 million living people and nearly 300,000 deceased. DMDC maintains over 60 million records and functions as the DoD's identity management provider, tying personnel to credentials used for access to Pentagon systems, buildings, and bases. The DoD said it has no indication the data was misused but offered no basis for that assessment, and the attackers remain unidentified. The incident follows the September 2026 ShinyHunters breach at the FBI and recalls the 2015 OPM breach of more than 22 million records attributed to China.
novelty: unencrypted PII of 3M+ military personnel exposed for 9 months
audience: security engineers and policy watchers tracking federal breach patterns
